**Windows get glass.** DOOM's maps are full of windows the original engine
could never glaze. They are now found in each map's geometry as it loads
(89 across DOOM's episodes, 77 in DOOM II) and get a pane of glass: grime
gathered along the frame and on the sill, shine streaks painted on it the
way Duke Nukem 3D painted its windows, and sharp highlights from lamps,
muzzle flashes and your flashlight.

**And it shatters.** The first bullet, fireball or rocket through a window
breaks it into a burst of glinting pixel shards that fall, bounce and lie on
the floor for a while, leaving a jagged rim in the frame. Explosions nearby
break windows too. Monsters' shots count as well, so a firefight across a
window leaves it in pieces. It is purely visual: shots, sight and movement
work exactly as in vanilla DOOM, and every level starts with its windows
whole.

**Windows reflect.** The window you look at mirrors the room in front of it:
the walls, the lamps, monsters coming up behind you, your own shots and you
yourself, at the same chunky resolution as the liquid reflections. Every
other window reflects a snapshot of its surroundings taken when the level
loads. Bright things show in the glass and dim walls stay faint, so a
window never turns into a mirror you can't see through.

**New in F4 > Textures > Surface detail:** Window glass, and under it Glass
reflections. Both are on by default. Reflections cost about 2–3 ms per frame
on a recent Mac, and only while you're looking at a window.

**Colored rooms.** Light from colored lamps, bounced around a room, now tints
its corners too, even where the lamps never reach directly. The new "Room
color from bounce" slider sets how strongly.

**Smaller touches.** Faintly painted seams in floor and wall artwork get
deeper bump detail. Teleport fog lights up its surroundings. Stair risers and
ledges shade the floor at their foot. The fog haze takes on the sky's color,
so it turns red under Inferno's sky.
